citation.title: Mental Models of Autonomy and Sentience Shape Reactions to AI
citation.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1–25; supplied arXiv v2

reading.source_scope_note: Three pilots (374 participations) and four randomized preregistered U.S. Prolific vignette experiments (2702 retained main-study participants) describe a fictional assistant's autonomy/sentience. Outcomes are immediate perceptions, moral-treatment beliefs, general harm judgments and ban preferences. The study does not establish actual AI sentience, measured real-world behavior or an identified causal mediator.
access_limits: All supplied pages and main plots read. OSF pilot details, full stimulus/item sets, preregistration histories, factor/path analyses, raw data, code and sampling-covariance choices are external and were not independently inspected.

Main studies exclude prior main-study participants; pilots exclude participation in another pilot. Independence across pilot and main pools is not explicitly established in the supplied main text. Do not call all 3076 combined participations independently unique people.
The original cited books, scales and previous empirical studies were not fully read here. Metadata checks and a reference title are not independent replications or source-paper credit.

study.pilots: Three preregistered Prolific pilot studies: free definitions/names N=124, capacity ranking N=100 and vignette testing N=150. They inform mappings of autonomy (independence, goals, control) and sentience (feeling, awareness, cognition and affect). Pilot participants cannot join another pilot. Detailed outputs are external, so this review does not independently reproduce their content analysis.
study.main_sample_flow: Experiment 1 recruits 274, excludes 20 attention failures, retains 254 (125 no-autonomy/129 autonomy). The extracted 2741 is 274 plus superscript footnote 1, not 2741 people. Experiment 2 recruits 276, excludes 20, retains 256 (133 no-sentience/123 sentience), excluding prior Experiment 1 participants. Experiment 3 recruits 765, excludes 24, retains 741 (None 185/Autonomy 200/Sentience 183/Both 173), excluding prior main participants. Experiment 4 recruits 1530, excludes 66 attention failures and 13 records lost to an unknown technical error, retains 1451 (382/358/343/368). Main retained sum 2702.
study.attention_and_population: Experiments 3/4 accept near-maximum slider responses intended as 7: 36 and 77 retained cases respectively. Exact rules/preregistration comparison need the external materials. Samples are U.S. Prolific adults, roughly half women, 68–72% White and somewhat liberal; participant characteristics are not a nationally representative inference. Interview/collection dates are not fully specified, and the authors discuss changed media context as an alternative explanation across experiments.
study.manipulations: Fictional smart assistant Corion is described with autonomy versus no autonomy in Experiment 1, sentience versus none in Experiment 2, and a 2×2 crossing in Experiments 3/4. Autonomy bundles independent activation, inner goals/motivation and choosing actions; sentience bundles sensing, information processing, moods and feelings with a positive breeze/pleasure example. All read a workday involving being blamed for a mistake and working overtime. Experiment 4 removes explicit conceptual labels but is a separate sample/study, not a randomized label-removal arm within one experiment.
study.measures: Six-item perceived-autonomy and perceived-sentience indices plus an established six-item cognitive/emotive mind scale, each 0–100. Moral Treatment six items and Scope of Justice three items concern AI in general, not only Corion. Harm concerns possible harm to people/future generations. AI Caution consists of three specific advanced-development bans, including sentience and AI-enhanced humans, not every possible governance policy. Scale orders/items randomized. Reliability is reported; strong construct overlap and valence/demand explanations remain possible.
study.experiment_1: Autonomy manipulation: perceived autonomy 74.74 versus 11.58, |d|=3.20. It also increases mind 52.58 versus 24.12, |d|=1.47; sentience 39.96 versus 10.12, |d|=1.30; Moral Treatment 3.44/2.81, p<.001; Scope of Justice 3.16/2.61, p=.008; Harm 4.44/3.96, p=.025. Ban preference 3.91/3.68 is nonsignificant, p=.335. Negative d and confidence intervals in the text arise from contrast coding, not a reversal of the displayed means.
study.experiment_2: Sentience manipulation: perceived sentience 69.37/6.45, |d|=2.91; perceived autonomy 58.22/21.09, |d|=1.64; mind 69.57/24.90, |d|=2.14. Scope of Justice 2.91/2.50, p=.036; Harm 4.47/3.95, p=.011; ban preferences 4.23/3.64, p=.016. Moral Treatment 3.13/2.79 has p=.054 and is explicitly nonsignificant at .05. Keep its suggestive direction separate from the significant justice outcome.
study.experiment_3: Both manipulations strongly affect their target perceptions; cross-effects are smaller (sentience→autonomy partial eta² .05; autonomy→sentience .02). Both raise mind, but mind interaction p=.114. Autonomy raises treatment p=.002, while justice p=.060 is nonsignificant; sentience raises both. Moral Treatment interaction p=.100 is nonsignificant; justice interaction p=.031. FDR-adjusted pairwise results support low None ratings, not a universal strongest Both effect. Autonomy raises harm, p=.001; sentience does not, p=.822. Autonomy ban effect p=.401 is null; sentience decreases bans, p=.037, opposite Experiment 2. No harm/ban interaction.
study.experiment_4: Without explicit labels, both manipulations again affect their target/cross-perceptions. Main mind effects partial eta² .11 autonomy/.49 sentience. Mind interaction p=.031, eta² .003; treatment interaction p=.003 and justice p=.001, each about eta² .01. None is lowest, but Both is not uniquely highest in moral consideration (H3b unsupported). Autonomy increases harm modestly, p=.043, eta² .003; sentience harm p=.230 is null. Both ban effects null (autonomy p=.936, sentience p=.869); harm/ban interactions null. Exploratory path analyses are external and do not independently identify causal mediators.
study.analysis_transparency: Preregistered ANCOVA analyses in Experiments 1/2 fail an assumption and are moved to the supplement; main text uses unadjusted comparisons and reports sensitivity consistency. The precise assumption/output was not inspected here. Experiments 3/4 omit those covariates and apply FDR to post hoc pairwise tests; this does not mean every main effect across seven outcomes is globally multiplicity-adjusted. Reported nulls and partial support are retained.
study.meta_analysis: Within-paper multivariate REML mixed-effects analysis of 42 effect sizes from four experiments, with study and outcome random effects. Forty-two estimates are not 42 independent studies; shared-participant/outcome covariance and small-study inferential choices need the external code. The paper reports autonomy d=.72, SE=.22, z=3.25, CI [.29,1.15] and sentience d=.92, SE=.24, z=3.80, CI [.45,1.40]. A comparison reports average d=.70/.90 and difference CI [−.26,−.16], with QM(2)=98.20. That omnibus statistic alone is not a specific one-degree comparison; retain the stated difference interval without claiming the uninspected model has been reproduced. Sensitivity excluding target-perception checks is reported as consistent, not independently verified.
study.scope: Randomization supports effects of descriptive bundles on immediate ratings, not actual autonomous/sentient capacities or a unique mental-representation mechanism. Strong sentience/mind correlations (.84–.89) and exploratory factor analyses do not establish metaphysical separability or causal ordering. The authors explicitly say the studies cannot settle metaphysics and note that sentient-but-not-autonomous targets may be harder to imagine. Attachment, therapy benefit, spillover mistreatment, interface tuning and literacy policies are implications, not outcomes tested here.

summary: Add perceived autonomy and mental modeling. Enrich existing experience/agency attribution and moral standing with randomized human-perception evidence; use existing social responses to computers and animism rather than duplicate labels. Preserve mixed threat/policy results, scale overlap, author-disclosed analytic changes and the difference between narrative effects and actual AI capacities.

findings.definition: Judging an entity as able to select and pursue goals or actions independently of external direction.
findings.origin: Human–AI interaction / perceptions of self-government and independent action
findings.ai_evidence_status: Directly measured human judgment about a fictional AI under randomized descriptive manipulations. This does not establish the real system's independence, human-like self-determination or actual control over deployment.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an assistant accurately describes which actions and goal choices it can initiate without further human direction. Compare user perceptions with actual authorization, intervention paths and task constraints. Test independence separately from planning skill, human-like wording and subjective experience.
findings.novelty_rationale: Agency attribution concerns perceived intentional thought/planning/action; an intentional actor can still act under external direction. Perceived control concerns whose influence over an interaction or outcome is believed. Perceived autonomy here concerns the target's independence and self-direction, not the user's control or the target's consciousness.

evidence.quote: robots acting more or less independently
their own goals
acts completely independently from others

findings.evidence_scope: Six-item autonomy ratings assess self-control and choosing goals. Autonomy cues increase ratings strongly, and sentience cues increase them more modestly in crossed designs. These are perception effects from bundled facts, not demonstration of actual free will or AI moral subjecthood. The comparison remains one paper with multiple experiments.
findings.boundary: Independence, task competence, authorized discretion, ability to override and moral responsibility differ. A model saying it chooses freely is not evidence it can set its own governing objectives; a user can also overestimate independence from ordinary interface cues.

findings.definition: Constructing or using an internal representation of a situation or system to predict its behavior and guide inference or action.
findings.origin: Cognitive psychology / mental models in human–computer interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: The study interprets randomized capacity descriptions through a mental-model framework. It observes reported perceptions and attitudes, not the complete internal representations or a uniquely identified cognitive mechanism.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant maintains a coherent, evidence-based working representation of tools, people, constraints and changing task state. Compare its predictions with observations and assess updates after contradictory evidence. A fluent explanation or chain of thought is not automatically a faithful record of an internal model.
findings.novelty_rationale: A perfect-automation schema is one specific expectation; affordance perception recognizes action possibilities; analogy maps from another case. Mental modeling concerns the broader representation used to predict and guide action. Semantic priming is one activation phenomenon, not the entire representational process.

evidence.quote: internal simulations of external reality
for predicting AI systems’ behavior and making decisions.
maintenance and updating of mental models

findings.evidence_scope: Pilot mapping and randomized descriptions change users' target and generic-AI judgments. This supports the relevance of representations/expectations but does not uniquely separate model activation from learning explicit facts, demand or framing. Long-term maintenance/updating and original cognitive-theory sources are not independently evaluated here.
findings.boundary: A representation can be useful, partial or wrong. Do not equate every wording effect with a distinct model, every stated belief with its full content, or every internal representation with consciousness. Assess predictive accuracy, relevant structure and justified updating.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source's perceived-sentience construct substantially overlaps attributed experience. Preserve its operational distinction in a note instead of adding a near-synonymous second row.

evidence.quote: feel pain
sensory perception, information processing, feelings, emotions,
sentience is distinguishable from autonomy

findings.evidence_scope: Sentience cues strongly change subjective-experience ratings and also influence autonomy/mind judgments. The manipulation and six-item index mix sensing, processing and feeling; the authors argue their construct is not simply all experience and call for further study. Do not collapse sensing functionality, emotion expression and phenomenal feeling or add their paper as empirical evidence that the AI actually feels.
findings.boundary: A narrative claim, perceived feeling and actual capacity for experience are different. Neither participants' ratings nor a restrictive philosophical definition settles sentience. Preserve construct/item content rather than treating sentience and experience as universally exact synonyms.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: The mind/autonomy measures provide relevant perception evidence, while target independence and cognitive/emotive capacities require distinct labels.

evidence.quote: emotive and cognitive capacities
These three measures are conceptually related

findings.evidence_scope: An established six-item mind scale mixes cognitive and emotive capacities; perceived-autonomy and sentience indices are adapted from related mind measures. Reported correlations and exploratory factor analyses do not validate treating mind, agency, autonomy and experience as one entity. Randomized descriptions affect attributed capacities, not proven actual intentionality.
findings.boundary: Planning ability, independence, experience and moral accountability can come apart. A total mind score is not a direct moral-agency diagnosis or proof that every agency attribution is anthropomorphic error.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Moral Treatment and Scope of Justice directly measure forms of consideration already covered; do not add moral circle inclusion as another near-identical row.

evidence.quote: Moral consideration, or inclusion in the moral circle
Robots/AIs deserve to be treated with respect
considerations of fairness apply to robots/AIs too

findings.evidence_scope: Descriptions of one fictional assistant alter general-AI treatment/justice beliefs. Effects are generally small compared with target-perception manipulation checks. Experiment 2 treatment p=.054 and Experiment 3 autonomy→justice p=.060 are nonsignificant, while other consideration outcomes support effects. Both features do not universally produce uniquely greatest consideration; H3b is unsupported in Experiment 4.
findings.boundary: A public attitude, actual prosocial behavior, rightful moral status and legal rights are distinct. Null Both-versus-single-feature differences are not equivalence. Moral consideration can be studied without declaring a real AI sentient or making a normative rights conclusion.

findings.definition: Applying interpersonal social responses or conventions to a computer during interaction, similar to responses used with people.
findings.novelty_rationale: CASA is the source's existing social-script framework, not a new synonym or a directly tested automaticity mechanism in these vignette ratings.

evidence.quote: akin to humans and other social animals
CASA is theoretically

findings.evidence_scope: The paper uses Computers Are Social Actors as a background explanation and distinguishes it from anthropomorphism. Its current experiments measure explicit reported perceptions, not automatic politeness, reciprocity or unconscious scripts. Original CASA studies are not newly read, so this boundary note receives no extra direct CASA-paper credit.
findings.boundary: A social response does not require an explicit belief that a machine is human. Conversely, an anthropomorphic attribution need not be consciously intentional. Do not infer evolutionary automaticity from a self-report outcome alone.

findings.definition: Attributing life, vitality or a soul to nonhuman entities, including objects or features of nature.
findings.novelty_rationale: The techno-animism scale is a technology-specific application of the existing animism concept rather than a separately new behavior.

evidence.quote: AI systems can have souls
natural entities, and robots/AIs can interact with each other

findings.evidence_scope: Three techno-animism items are measured as covariates in Experiments 1/2, with reported alpha .71/.75. Main adjusted models fail an assumption and are presented externally. The paper does not manipulate animism or demonstrate that it causes the reported effects; this is relevant measurement/context evidence, not a causal animism test.
findings.boundary: Soul attribution, subjective experience, intelligent behavior and independent action differ. Cultural/religious beliefs are not diagnosed as errors merely because a technology is the target. Do not equate measured belief with a verified property of the AI.

findings.definition: An affective response to a perceived threat or possibility of harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source discusses threat, but its general harm ratings are not a direct fear-emotion measure. Preserve that distinction without counting the study as another direct fear experiment.

evidence.quote: Robots/AIs may be harmful to future generations
collapse across realistic and

findings.evidence_scope: Autonomy increases judgments that AI can harm people; sentience's harm effect is positive in Experiment 2 and null in Experiments 3/4. Policy preferences are another distinct outcome. The authors acknowledge their harm/ban measures collapse realistic and symbolic threat; they do not separately measure felt fear, threat subtypes or actual danger.
findings.boundary: Believing harm is possible, experiencing fear, supporting bans and estimating actual risk are different. A nonsignificant policy effect does not establish no influence on all governance preferences, nor should a risk judgment automatically be called irrational fear.

source_corrections.location: Figure 1 caption and broad sentience summary
source_corrections.issue: A blanket statement that autonomy and sentience increase threat can conceal the inconsistent sentience results shown in the table.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Autonomy increases perceived harm consistently; sentience increases it in Experiment 2 but not Experiments 3/4. Sentience increases ban preferences in Experiment 2, decreases them in Experiment 3 and has a null effect in Experiment 4. Preserve the figure's inconsistent labels and reported nulls/reversal rather than infer a universal threat/policy effect.

source_corrections.issue: The displayed z statistic does not yield p<.001 under the ordinary two-sided standard-normal test.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: For z=3.25, two-sided p≈.001154. Clarify whether a directional test, another statistic or a formatting error explains the label; the actual code was not inspected. The result remains significant at .01. Do not invent a corrected underlying estimate or claim the entire meta-analysis is invalid.

source_corrections.issue: QM with two degrees of freedom is presented alongside a comparison of autonomy and sentience.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: An omnibus two-parameter test alone does not establish a specific autonomy-versus-sentience difference. The reported difference interval may support that comparison, but its contrast and dependence model require the external code. Preserve the reported interval and distinguish four studies from 42 correlated estimates; no reanalysis is claimed.

source_corrections.issue: Anthropomorphism is characterized as intentional while CASA is characterized as unconscious.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Social-script application and attributed human-like mental capacities are distinct constructs, but conscious intention is not a universal necessary condition of anthropomorphism. The current ratings do not independently establish either process's automaticity. Retain the paper's theoretical distinction without turning it into an exclusive conscious/unconscious taxonomy.

source_corrections.issue: Statements about expert agreement, AI consciousness, therapy/literacy benefits and design tuning can exceed what these perception experiments establish.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The authors explicitly acknowledge that the studies cannot settle metaphysics and use hypothetical targets. Their referenced expert opinions and proposed interventions are distinct evidence. Do not transform participants' beliefs into actual sentience, a settled consensus across all experts or a clinically validated recommendation.

source_corrections.issue: Similar results across separately collected samples are described as robustness to labels.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: This is useful cross-study consistency, not a randomized isolated label effect or proof of equivalence. Time/context/sample and power differ; the authors themselves discuss changing media context and imagination difficulty as alternatives.

source_identity_checks.finding: The supplied bibliography prints Social Cognition 37(1):41–S2. Crossref for DOI 10.1521/soco.2019.37.1.41 repeats the same anomalous page range. Metadata repetition is not independent verification of the endpoint, so this review does not silently replace S2 with a guessed number.
source_identity_checks.scope: Identity/metadata check only; publisher full text and original page endpoint not independently verified.

source_identity_checks.location: Original cognitive/ethical books and public-sentience surveys
source_identity_checks.finding: Cited books, prior surveys and scales provide conceptual background; none is an independently completed full reading in this review. A meta-analysis of the present four studies is one article, not four or 42 independent paper citations for a behavior.
source_identity_checks.scope: Source types and relationships read in supplied paper; no external full-book or survey-data reanalysis.

methodological_limits: Randomized narrative bundles change immediate ratings of a fictional assistant. They do not uniquely identify a latent representation process or establish actual AI sentience, moral agency or rights.

The measures mix sensing, cognition, emotion and autonomy and are strongly correlated. The authors disclose exploratory factor work and acknowledge unresolved conceptual relationships; those external analyses were not independently read.
Main participants are mutually excluded across main studies and pilots across pilots. Cross-pool uniqueness is not established. All main samples are U.S. Prolific, not a representative global public.

The common blamed/overtime workday, positive sentience example and explicit descriptive facts can affect interpretation/demand. Equal clinical/ecological validity across all hypothetical combinations is not established.

Authors disclose moving preregistered adjusted analyses after an assumption failure, near-maximum attention-check retention and unknown technical missingness. External preregistrations/data/code were not audited.

Exploratory path models and within-paper aggregation do not create an identified mediator or independent replication. Sampling covariance and small-study meta-inference need the actual analysis files.

Some consideration effects are nonsignificant, and strongest-Both hypotheses only partly hold. Nonsignificance is not equivalence; a significant result in one study and a null in another is not a tested between-study difference.

Harm beliefs, emotional fear, actual risk, moral treatment beliefs, observed behavior and a narrow ban-policy scale remain separate. Design/therapy/literacy proposals were not experimentally evaluated.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The prior article adopts a restrictive normative position on moral agency; the present article measures human perceptions and explicitly disclaims metaphysical conclusions. Neither should be used to collapse actual agency, attributed mind and moral consideration into one construct.

Named ethical categories, explicit descriptive labels and generated text do not by themselves prove stable inner mechanisms. Here randomization provides stronger causal evidence for narrative effects than a selected-output comparison, while mediator and capacity claims still need separate evidence.

Accurate working representations matter for assigning feasible oversight roles. Perceived autonomy or a favorable analogy does not establish actual control, authorized authority or an effective maintenance intervention.

deferred.reason: Enrich experience attribution and moral standing rather than duplicate overlapping terms; preserve source-specific definitions and scale content in the notes.

deferred.term: Computers Are Social Actors and techno-animism
deferred.reason: Existing social responses to computers and animism cover the background framework and technology-specific belief scale. No new alias becomes an independent behavior.
Clearly defined theory leads, but the actual outcomes collapse them. Read the original threat-theory/measurement work before adding separately validated subtype entries.

A secondary cited finding about reweighting what makes humans distinctive. Its original Santoro/Monin study was not read; do not confuse it with the different historical use of AI effect for dismissing solved computational tasks.

deferred.term: AI attachment, intergroup spillover and policy tuning
deferred.reason: Related literature and implications, not directly measured attachment, transfer to human treatment, literacy benefit or prompt-policy effectiveness in these four studies.

limitations: Two additions and existing-entry notes retain human-perception evidence versus proposed AI evaluations. No automatic violation/harm edges, invented yearly series or three-paper quota.
The accepted arXiv version and canonical proceedings identity refer to the same work and are not independent papers. Books, related papers and uninspected supplements do not receive full-read credit.
The existing catalogue/ontology is updated in place on the draft research branch with stable IDs and eleven categories; no live merge or deployment is performed.
